objects: incomplete matrix X; target matrix Z; observed index set Omega
assumptions: high-dimensional matrix with few observed entries
conclusion: Matrix completion seeks to infer an underlying matrix from a small subset of its entries.
scope: Motivating inverse problem, rather than an identifiability guarantee.
span: In many applications measured data can be represented in a matrix Xm×n, for which only a relatively small number of entries are observed. The problem is to “complete” the matrix based on the observed entries, and has been dubbed the matrix completion problem [CCS08, CR08, RFP07, CT09, KOM09, RS05].

span: In this paper, as is relevant in many real life applications, we assume that Z can be well represented by a matrix of low rank, i.e. Z ≈ Vm×kGk×n, where k ≪ min(n, m).

assumptions: model chosen by a criterion such as cross-validation
conclusion: Shrinkage can cause the selected matrix to retain more singular values than the true underlying rank.
scope: Author-stated rank-selection limitation and motivation for post-processing.
span: Because the ℓ1 norm regularizes by shrinking the singular values, the number of singular values retained (through cross-validation, say) may exceed the actual rank of the matrix. In such cases it is reasonable to undo the shrinkage of the chosen models, which might permit a lower-rank solution.
